front_matter.title: Positivity (P) as additive weights on effects (reading argued); parity average adds none
front_matter.subject: clifford-structure

extraction.note: The first and third attack items of op.positivity-of-values, constructive side: what (P) is equivalent to, and whether the descent supplies it. Clause (ii) is the theorem of P. Busch (Quantum states and generalized observables: a simple proof of Gleason's theorem, Phys. Rev. Lett. 91 (2003) 120403, arXiv:quant-ph/9909073; existence, title and abstract checked on the web, the argument from memory) and of Caves, Fuchs, Manne and Renes (Found. Phys. 34 (2004) 193, from memory), placed in the series' algebra with the blade inverse and stated over ordered fields; over the rationals the linear extension needs no positivity and no continuity, a remark that is probably known and is not claimed as new. Clause (iv) is the standard fact that a group average is a positive map. Clause (v) is an identity in the algebra of two modes; the stored CHSH bound, clause (viii), already records that a saturating state can be even. What this result records about the open problem. (1) (P) is not derived from the stored measurement premises; it is shown equivalent to a strong form of the residual postulate that the stored Born account isolates (one-relation.measure-indifference-borns-rule-located: that weights exist and add), namely non-negative normalised weights on all effects that add whenever the sum is an effect. That this is the right reading of the residual postulate is argued, not proved: the stored postulate is informal, and its weak reading (additivity for projectors of one commuting family) does not give (P) when atoms come in complementary pairs (Gleason's theorem excludes dimension two; the stored result on weights on projectors, synthesis.no-two-valued-weights-on-the-atoms-of-two-modes-the-even-subalgebra-admits-them, treats that case for two modes, and clause (iii) here is one instance used only to show an effect relation at work). (2) The parity average of the descent maps positive elements to positive elements and creates no positivity, so "the descent is a conditional expectation" gives (P) only for functionals already positive on even elements; under the univalence premise (singularity.p-univalence) (P) is a statement about the even subalgebra. The stored result synthesis.local-weights-give-the-chsh-bound-and-do-not-fix-positivity-of-values treats the mode-wise and total parity averages on two modes with the box functional (its clause (v), which cites clause (iv) here, the general lemma). The case of parity-homogeneous directions in clause (v) (at most 2) is treated with the sector average of an observable in synthesis.records-keep-even-states-even-only-for-parity-homogeneous-observables (its clause (iii)). Atoms, sharp states and their uniqueness are those of the stored base synthesis.born-weights-under-positivity-a-state-sharp-on-an-atom-is-its-trace-functional, cited in clauses (iii) and (v) and not re-proved. (3) Univalence and the parity average act on states and on single elements; they do not remove the correlations of parity-odd elements, so they do not decide between the two stored settings for observables. The independence statement that these clauses support is limited: positivity is independent of linearity, normalisation, reality, evenness and invariance under the parity average, on one algebra; independence from the whole stored premise set is not claimed. Kill conditions registered before computing: 1 fails to be an order unit for the cone of hermitian squares, or the extension is not well defined (neither occurred); an even state cannot exceed 2 at one mode per party with the Klein-twisted directions (it reaches 14/5). Classical mathematics; transport-absent.

levels.formal:
Let $k$ be $\Q$ or an ordered field, and $\Cl_{k}(p,q)$, the blade inverse $\dagger$ and the scalar part $\langle\cdot\rangle_{0}$ as in Theorem \claimref{synthesis.chsh-bound-for-two-subsystems-of-a-clifford-algebra-by-a-rational-certificate}, for a fixed split of the generators. Premise (P), positivity of values (Premise \claimref{synthesis.premise-positivity-of-values}), is assumed, not derived, wherever states are spoken of: a \emph{state} is a $k$-linear $\omega$ with $\omega(1) = 1$, $\omega(xx^{\dagger}) \ge 0$ and $\omega(x^{\dagger}) = \omega(x)$.

\emph{Definitions.} The \emph{cone} $\mathcal{K}$ is the set of sums $\sum_{r}c_{r}x_{r}x_{r}^{\dagger}$ with $c_{r} \ge 0$ in $k$. An \emph{effect} is an element $E$ with $E \in \mathcal{K}$ and $1 - E \in \mathcal{K}$; projectors (elements $E = E^{\dagger} = E^{2}$) are effects. A \emph{weight} is a map $\mu$ from effects to $k$ with $\mu(E) \ge 0$, $\mu(1) = 1$, and $\mu(E + F) = \mu(E) + \mu(F)$ whenever $E$, $F$ and $E + F$ are effects.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(The unit bounds every self-adjoint element; proved.)} The self-adjoint elements are the span of the blades of square $1$. For such a blade $b$, $1 \pm b = \tfrac12(1 \pm b)(1 \pm b)^{\dagger}$. Hence for self-adjoint $s = \sum_{b}c_{b}b$ and $n_{s} = \sum_{b}|c_{b}|$ both $n_{s} - s$ and $n_{s} + s$ lie in $\mathcal{K}$; every self-adjoint element is a difference of two elements of $\mathcal{K}$, and the effects span the self-adjoint elements.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(Weights on effects are the states of (P); proved for $k = \Q$ and for every Archimedean ordered $k$.)} The restriction of a state to the effects is a weight, and every weight is the restriction of exactly one state. For $k = \Q$ the non-negativity of $\mu$ is not used in showing that $\mu$ extends to a linear functional: every map on effects with values in $\Q$ that is additive in the sense above extends uniquely to a $\Q$-linear functional $\omega$ with $\omega(x^{\dagger}) = \omega(x)$, and it is non-negative on effects exactly when $\omega(xx^{\dagger}) \ge 0$ for all $x$. So (P) is equivalent to: values of effects are non-negative, normalised and additive.
\item[(iii)] \emph{(An effect relation at work; proved, one instance.)} On one mode, $\Cl_{k}(1,1)$ with $p_{1} = f_{1}e_{1}$, let $\Pi_{e} = \tfrac12(1 + e_{1})$, $\Pi_{p} = \tfrac12(1 + p_{1})$, $E_{a} = \tfrac12(1 + \tfrac35 e_{1} + \tfrac45 p_{1})$, three projectors. Then $\tfrac12E_{a} + \tfrac{1}{10} = \tfrac{3}{10}\Pi_{e} + \tfrac{4}{10}\Pi_{p}$, with every term and both sides effects. A weight with $\mu(\Pi_{p}) = 1$ and $\mu(\Pi_{e}) = \tfrac12$ therefore has $\mu(E_{a}) = \tfrac{9}{10}$. By (ii) and clause (iii) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.born-weights-under-positivity-a-state-sharp-on-an-atom-is-its-trace-functional}, every weight with $\mu(\Pi_{p}) = 1$ is the restriction of the one state sharp on the atom $\Pi_{p}$, $x \mapsto 2\langle\Pi_{p}x\rangle_{0}$, so both values hold for it; the relation shows how additivity on effects carries the second value to the third. The function $\tfrac12(1 + xe_{1} + zp_{1}) \mapsto \tfrac12(1 + z^{3})$ on the projectors other than $0$ and $1$ is non-negative, takes those two values, and is additive on every pair of projectors with sum $1$, the only families of orthogonal projectors of one mode; it gives $E_{a}$ the value $\tfrac{189}{250}$ and so is not the restriction of a weight on effects.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(The parity average keeps the cone and adds no positivity; proved.)} Let $\Gamma$ be self-adjoint with $\Gamma^{2} = 1$ and $E_{\Gamma}(x) = \tfrac12(x + \Gamma x\Gamma)$, the average of Theorem \claimref{singularity.descent-parity-average} (there for one mode; for the total parity as in Theorem \claimref{synthesis.mode-split-of-the-clifford-algebra-and-its-klein-twist-to-the-tensor-product}). Then $E_{\Gamma}(x^{\dagger}) = E_{\Gamma}(x)^{\dagger}$, $E_{\Gamma}(yy^{\dagger}) = \tfrac12\bigl(yy^{\dagger} + (\Gamma y)(\Gamma y)^{\dagger}\bigr)$, and $E_{\Gamma}(\mathcal{K})$ is the set of elements of $\mathcal{K}$ fixed by $E_{\Gamma}$. So for a linear functional $\varphi$, $\varphi \circ E_{\Gamma}$ is non-negative on $\mathcal{K}$ exactly when $\varphi$ is non-negative on the fixed elements of $\mathcal{K}$: a functional invariant under the average satisfies the positivity clause only if it is already non-negative on the fixed positive elements, and the average does not make it so. Example: on $\Cl_{k}(2,2)$, $\varphi(x) = \langle(1 + 2p_{1})x\rangle_{0}$ is linear, normalised, real and invariant under the total parity average, with $\varphi(\tfrac12(1 - p_{1})) = -\tfrac12$. Rider: averaging over more involutions leaves fewer fixed elements. In $\Cl_{k}(\ell,\ell)$ the composition of the averages over the mode parities $p_{1}, \dots, p_{\ell}$ has as fixed elements the span of the $2^{\ell}$ orthogonal projectors $\prod_{j}\tfrac12(1 \pm p_{j})$, and a normalised functional invariant under it satisfies the positivity clause exactly when its $2^{\ell}$ values on these projectors are non-negative: for the mode-wise average (P) reduces to finitely many non-negative weights, while for the total parity alone it does not. For the grading automorphism $\alpha$ of $\Cl_{k}(p,q)$, $p + q \ge 1$ (the map that fixes even and negates odd elements; in a general signature it need not be conjugation by a self-adjoint element of square $1$), and $E = \tfrac12(\mathrm{id} + \alpha)$, the same statements hold, and the fixed elements of $\mathcal{K}$ are the sums $\sum_{r}c_{r}y_{r}y_{r}^{\dagger}$ with every $y_{r}$ even: for a functional that vanishes on odd elements, (P) on the algebra is equivalent to (P) for its restriction to the even subalgebra. This, and the statement that $\omega \circ E$ is a state when $\omega$ is, is clause (i) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.univalence-even-extension-split} (for the completed mode algebra: $\omega \circ E$ is the one even state agreeing with $\omega$ on the even part), here over $k$ with the blade inverse; what is added is that the hermitian squares of odd elements are hermitian squares of even ones.
\item[(v)] \emph{(Even states see the products of odd directions; proved, under (P) for the inequality.)} In $\Cl_{k}(2,2)$ let $\Gamma = p_{1}p_{2}$ and take the directions of clause (vii) of the theorem cited first, $a_{i} = x_{i}e_{1} + z_{i}p_{1}$ and $b_{j} = x'_{j}e_{2}p_{1} + z'_{j}p_{2}$ ($x_{i}^{2} + z_{i}^{2} = x'^{2}_{j} + z'^{2}_{j} = 1$), with CHSH element $C = a_{1}(b_{1} + b_{2}) + a_{2}(b_{1} - b_{2})$. Put $X = x_{1}(x'_{1} + x'_{2}) + x_{2}(x'_{1} - x'_{2})$, $Z = z_{1}(z'_{1} + z'_{2}) + z_{2}(z'_{1} - z'_{2})$ and $u = e_{2}f_{1}$. Then
\[
E_{\Gamma}(C) = Xu + Z\Gamma, \qquad u^{\dagger} = u, \quad u^{2} = 1, \quad u\Gamma = \Gamma u ,
\]
while the CHSH element of the averaged directions $E_{\Gamma}(a_{i}) = z_{i}p_{1}$, $E_{\Gamma}(b_{j}) = z'_{j}p_{2}$ is $Z\Gamma$: the average is not multiplicative, $E_{\Gamma}(a_{i}b_{j}) \ne E_{\Gamma}(a_{i})E_{\Gamma}(b_{j})$ when $x_{i}x'_{j} \ne 0$. For every state $\omega$ with $\omega \circ E_{\Gamma} = \omega$ (an even state): $\omega(C) = X\omega(u) + Z\omega(\Gamma)$ and $|\omega(C)| \le |X| + |Z|$, with equality on the four even projectors $\tfrac14(1 \pm u)(1 \pm \Gamma)$ for suitable signs (atoms in the sense of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.born-weights-under-positivity-a-state-sharp-on-an-atom-is-its-trace-functional}, clause (i), the blades $u$, $\Gamma$ being a maximal independent commuting set), and $(|X| + |Z|)^{2} \le 8$. At $a_{1} = e_{1}$, $a_{2} = p_{1}$, $b_{1} = \tfrac35 e_{2}p_{1} + \tfrac45 p_{2}$, $b_{2} = \tfrac45 e_{2}p_{1} - \tfrac35 p_{2}$: $X = Z = \tfrac75$, the even state of $\tfrac14(1 + u)(1 + \Gamma)$ has $\omega(C) = \tfrac{14}{5} > 2$, and the averaged directions give at most $\tfrac75$. The value above $2$ uses directions of mixed parity ($b_{1}$, $b_{2}$ have an odd and an even part); when every direction is even or odd ($x_{i}z_{i} = 0$ and $x'_{j}z'_{j} = 0$) one checks from the formula that $|X| + |Z| \le 2$. So a restriction to even states (Premise \claimref{singularity.p-univalence}, which is not assumed here) together with the parity average does not reduce the setting with parity-odd directions to the setting with parity-even observables; only a restriction on which elements are observables would.
\end{enumerate}
\emph{Scope.} Clause (ii) does not derive (P); it says what (P) is equivalent to, and over $\Q$ it is close to a restatement: non-negativity on effects is the positivity clause and additivity is linearity. Its content is the reading of the stored residual postulate (weights exist and add) as additivity over all effects; that reading is argued, effects that are not projectors are not outcomes of the stored record account, and additivity over effects that do not commute is the non-contextuality assumption again. So the content of the envariance argument (Zurek; prior art of the stored Born account) is relocated into (P), not reduced. The equivalent statement is strong: additivity is asked of all effects, including sums of effects that do not commute, which no single measurement realises. Clause (iv) is about one algebra and the positivity clause; it does not show that (P) is independent of the series' other premises.
levels.technical:
Premise (P), positivity of values, is assumed in the series and not derived. This result says what it is equivalent to and what the descent does for it, in every Clifford algebra $\Cl_{k}(p,q)$ over the rationals or an Archimedean ordered field, with the blade inverse as adjoint. Call an element an effect if it and its complement to $1$ are combinations, with non-negative coefficients, of elements $xx^{\dagger}$; projectors are effects, and so are their multiples by numbers between $0$ and $1$. Then the states of (P) are exactly the assignments of non-negative numbers to effects that give $1$ the value $1$ and add whenever a sum of two effects is an effect. Over the rationals additivity alone already gives linearity, with no continuity argument; non-negativity then is the positivity clause. So, given this reading, (P) is the statement that weights exist on all effects, are non-negative and add; it is a strong form of the residual postulate that the stored Born account isolates, and it is strong because it asks additivity also of effects that do not commute. A relation among effects of one mode shows the mechanism: it forces the weight $\tfrac{9}{10}$ where a function that is additive only on complementary projectors can give $\tfrac{189}{250}$.

The parity average of the descent, $x \mapsto \tfrac12(x + \Gamma x\Gamma)$, commutes with the adjoint and maps positive elements to positive elements, so it preserves states (for the completed mode algebra this is clause (i) of the stored even-extension theorem); but it creates no positivity. A functional invariant under the average satisfies the positivity clause only if it is already non-negative on the positive even elements, and a normalised real invariant functional can give a projector the value $-\tfrac12$. For functionals that vanish on odd elements, (P) is a statement about the even subalgebra alone. Finally, under (P), the average is not multiplicative: for the stored one-mode directions of mixed parity against the Klein-twisted other mode, the average of the CHSH element is $Xu + Z\Gamma$ with $u = e_{2}f_{1}$ even, and an even state gives it values up to $|X| + |Z|$, for example $\tfrac{14}{5}$, where the CHSH element of the averaged directions gives at most $\tfrac75$. So restricting states to even ones and applying the average does not turn the setting with parity-odd directions into the setting with even observables; that would take a restriction on observables.
levels.lay:
The series assumes a rule, called (P), for the averages of measurable quantities: averages add up, the trivial quantity has average 1, and a quantity times its mirror image never has a negative average. This result shows, under that reading of the terms, what the assumption amounts to. Think of every yes-or-no question, sharp or blurred, as having a chance. Then (P) holds exactly when those chances are never negative, the certain question has chance 1, and the chances add up whenever two questions combine into one. Over fractions nothing more is needed, not even an argument about limits. So (P) is the assumption that chances exist and add, in a strong form: the adding is required even for questions that cannot be asked in the same experiment.

Two further points, both given the series' stated definitions. The series has an averaging step, part of what it calls the descent, that erases quantities which change the count of particles from even to odd. Assuming nothing beyond its definition, that step keeps non-negative averages non-negative, but it cannot produce the property where it is absent, so (P) cannot be obtained from it. And although the step erases each such quantity on its own, it does not erase the product of two of them, which is of the even kind. Under (P), a state that respects the even-odd rule can still show correlations of 2.8 between two parties who use such quantities, above the limit of 2 that holds, with one mode for each party, when they do not; this needs quantities that mix the even and the odd kind. So the even-odd rule for states does not settle whether such quantities count as measurements.
levels.one-liner: Under the stated definitions, in $\Cl_{k}(p,q)$ over $\Q$ or an Archimedean ordered field: the states of (P) are exactly the non-negative, normalised, additive weights on effects (over $\Q$ additivity alone gives linearity; close to a restatement of (P), and that the stored postulate that weights exist and add means this, for effects that do not commute, is argued, not proved); the parity average maps positive elements to positive elements and creates no positivity; and for even states the CHSH element of mixed-parity directions has the value of $Xu + Z\Gamma$, up to $|X| + |Z|$ (for example $\tfrac{14}{5}$), not that of the averaged directions.

proofs.main:
\emph{Preliminaries.} Write $\tau = \langle\cdot\rangle_{0}$. By Theorem \claimref{synthesis.signed-directions-and-the-integer-clifford-algebra} the blades are a basis and each blade $b$ has $b^{-1} = \pm b$, so $b^{\dagger} = b$ exactly when $b^{2} = 1$ and $b^{\dagger} = -b$ otherwise; $\dagger$ is an anti-automorphism, and $\tau(x^{\dagger}x)$ is the sum of the squares of the coefficients of $x$ (clause (iii) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.chsh-bound-for-two-subsystems-of-a-clifford-algebra-by-a-rational-certificate}). The cone $\mathcal{K}$ is closed under sums and under multiplication by non-negative elements of $k$, and contains $1 = 1 \cdot 1^{\dagger}$ and every projector $E = EE^{\dagger}$; if $E$ is a projector so is $1 - E$, so projectors are effects. Two remarks used below. (A) If $E$ is an effect and $0 \le t \le 1$ in $k$, then $tE$ is an effect, since $1 - tE = t(1 - E) + (1 - t)$. (B) If $c, c' \in \mathcal{K}$ and $c + c'$ is an effect, then $c$ and $c'$ are effects, since $1 - c = (1 - c - c') + c'$.

\emph{(i).} The self-adjoint elements are the span of the self-adjoint blades because $\dagger$ multiplies each blade by $\pm 1$. For a blade $b$ of square $1$, $(1 \pm b)^{\dagger} = 1 \pm b$ and $(1 \pm b)^{2} = 2(1 \pm b)$. For $s = \sum_{b}c_{b}b$ (the scalar blade included), $n_{s} - s = \sum_{b}|c_{b}|\,(1 - \operatorname{sgn}(c_{b})\,b)$, and each term is $|c_{b}|$ times an element $\tfrac12(1 \mp b)(1 \mp b)^{\dagger}$ (for the scalar blade the term is $0$ or $2|c_{b}|$); likewise $n_{s} + s$. So $s = \tfrac12(n_{s} + s) - \tfrac12(n_{s} - s)$ is a difference of elements of $\mathcal{K}$, and for $s \ne 0$ the element $(n_{s} + s)/(2n_{s})$ is an effect, with complement $(n_{s} - s)/(2n_{s})$, so $s$ is a combination of that effect and of the effect $1$.

\emph{(ii).} A state restricts to a weight: non-negativity on $\mathcal{K}$ is the positivity clause with linearity, and additivity is linearity. Conversely let $\mu$ be a weight. Step 1: for an effect $E$ and integers $0 \le j \le n$, $n \ge 1$, the elements $jE/n$ are effects by (A), so additivity gives $\mu(jE/n) = j\mu(E/n)$ and $\mu(E) = n\mu(E/n)$: $\mu(rE) = r\mu(E)$ for rational $r \in [0,1]$. Step 2, used only when $k \ne \Q$: for $t \in k$ with $0 \le t \le 1$ and rationals $r \le t \le r'$ in $[0,1]$, $\mu(tE) = \mu(rE) + \mu((t - r)E) \ge r\mu(E)$ and $\mu(r'E) = \mu(tE) + \mu((r' - t)E) \ge \mu(tE)$, by additivity and non-negativity; so $\mu(tE)$ and $t\mu(E)$ both lie between $r\mu(E)$ and $r'\mu(E)$, and since $k$ is Archimedean $r' - r$ can be made smaller than any positive element, whence $\mu(tE) = t\mu(E)$. Step 3: for $c \in \mathcal{K}$ there is an integer $n \ge 1$ with $c/n$ an effect: by (i) $n_{c} - c \in \mathcal{K}$, and any integer $n \ge n_{c}$ (which exists as $k$ is Archimedean) has $1 - c/n = \bigl((n_{c} - c) + (n - n_{c})\bigr)/n \in \mathcal{K}$. Put $\omega(c) = n\mu(c/n)$; by Step 1 this does not depend on $n$ (compare $n$ and $n'$ through $nn'$). For $c, c' \in \mathcal{K}$ choose $n$ with $(c + c')/n$ an effect; by (B) $c/n$ and $c'/n$ are effects and additivity of $\mu$ gives $\omega(c + c') = \omega(c) + \omega(c')$. By Steps 1 and 2, $\omega(tc) = t\omega(c)$ for $t \ge 0$ in $k$, and $\omega \ge 0$ on $\mathcal{K}$. Step 4: by (i) every self-adjoint $s$ is $c - c'$ with $c, c' \in \mathcal{K}$; put $\omega(s) = \omega(c) - \omega(c')$, well defined because $c - c' = d - d'$ gives $c + d' = d + c'$ and additivity on $\mathcal{K}$ applies. This $\omega$ is $k$-linear on the self-adjoint elements. Step 5: put $\omega(x) = \omega(\tfrac12(x + x^{\dagger}))$ for all $x$. Then $\omega$ is $k$-linear, $\omega(x^{\dagger}) = \omega(x)$, $\omega(xx^{\dagger}) \ge 0$ because $xx^{\dagger} \in \mathcal{K}$, $\omega(1) = \mu(1) = 1$, and $\omega = \mu$ on effects (take $n = 1$): $\omega$ is a state in the sense of Premise \claimref{synthesis.premise-positivity-of-values}. Uniqueness: two states that agree on effects agree on their span, the self-adjoint elements, and the reality clause gives $\omega(x) = \omega(\tfrac12(x + x^{\dagger}))$. For $k = \Q$ Step 2 is not needed, and Steps 1, 3, 4, 5 use only additivity: they give a $\Q$-linear real $\omega$ for any additive map on effects with values in $\Q$; then $\omega(xx^{\dagger}) \ge 0$ for all $x$ exactly when $\mu \ge 0$ on effects, because every element of $\mathcal{K}$ is a positive integer multiple of an effect.

\emph{(iii).} $\tfrac{3}{10}\Pi_{e} + \tfrac{4}{10}\Pi_{p} = \tfrac{7}{20} + \tfrac{3}{20}e_{1} + \tfrac{4}{20}p_{1} = \tfrac12E_{a} + \tfrac{1}{10}$. Each term is a multiple of a projector or of $1$ by a number in $[0,1]$, hence an effect by (A), and the common value is an effect because its complement is $\tfrac12(1 - E_{a}) + \tfrac{4}{10} \in \mathcal{K}$; so by (B) the partial sums are effects and additivity applies to both sides: $\tfrac12\mu(E_{a}) + \tfrac{1}{10} = \tfrac{3}{10}\mu(\Pi_{e}) + \tfrac{4}{10}\mu(\Pi_{p})$, using Step 1 of (ii) for the rational multiples. With the two given values, $\mu(E_{a}) = \tfrac{9}{10}$. $\Pi_{p}$ is the vacuum projector of one mode, an atom by clause (i) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.born-weights-under-positivity-a-state-sharp-on-an-atom-is-its-trace-functional}; a weight with $\mu(\Pi_{p}) = 1$ extends by (ii) to a state sharp on it, which by clause (iii) of that theorem is $x \mapsto 2\tau(\Pi_{p}x)$, with values $\tfrac12$ on $\Pi_{e}$ and $\tfrac{9}{10}$ on $E_{a}$. Here $\Cl_{k}(1,1)$ is one mode in the sense of Proposition \claimref{tower.ladder-pairs-satisfy-car-vectors}, with generators $e_{1}$, $f_{1}$ of squares $1$, $-1$. Its self-adjoint elements are the span of $1$, $e_{1}$, $p_{1}$ (by (i): $f_{1}^{2} = -1$), and $\tfrac12(1 + n)$ with $n = xe_{1} + zp_{1}$ is idempotent exactly when $n^{2} = x^{2} + z^{2} = 1$ (the elements $e_{1}$, $p_{1}$ anticommute), while an idempotent $c + \tfrac12 n'$ with $c \ne \tfrac12$ forces $n' = 0$ and $c \in \{0, 1\}$; two such projectors $\tfrac12(1 + n)$, $\tfrac12(1 + n')$ have product zero only if $n' = -n$. So the families of orthogonal nonzero projectors are the pairs $\{E, 1 - E\}$, and a function $g$ on these projectors is additive on them exactly when $g(\tfrac12(1 - n)) = 1 - g(\tfrac12(1 + n))$, which holds for $\tfrac12(1 + z^{3})$ since $z \mapsto z^{3}$ is odd; it is non-negative because $|z| \le 1$. Its values $1$, $\tfrac12$, $\tfrac{189}{250}$ are the script's, and $\tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac{189}{250} + \tfrac{1}{10} = \tfrac{239}{500} \ne \tfrac{275}{500}$.

\emph{(iv).} $\Gamma^{\dagger} = \Gamma$ gives $(\Gamma x\Gamma)^{\dagger} = \Gamma x^{\dagger}\Gamma$, so $E_{\Gamma}$ commutes with $\dagger$; and $\Gamma yy^{\dagger}\Gamma = (\Gamma y)(\Gamma y)^{\dagger}$. Hence $E_{\Gamma}(\mathcal{K}) \subset \mathcal{K}$, every element of $E_{\Gamma}(\mathcal{K})$ is fixed because $E_{\Gamma}$ is idempotent (Theorem \claimref{singularity.descent-parity-average} for one mode; in general $\Gamma^{2} = 1$ gives $E_{\Gamma}E_{\Gamma} = E_{\Gamma}$), and a fixed element $c$ of $\mathcal{K}$ is $E_{\Gamma}(c)$. The statement about $\varphi \circ E_{\Gamma}$ follows. In the example $1 + 2p_{1}$ is self-adjoint and commutes with the total parity $p_{1}p_{2}$ of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.mode-split-of-the-clifford-algebra-and-its-klein-twist-to-the-tensor-product}, so $\varphi$ is real and invariant; $\varphi(\tfrac12(1 - p_{1})) = \tfrac12(1 - 2) = -\tfrac12$, and $\tfrac12(1 - p_{1})$ is a projector. Rider: the averages over the commuting self-adjoint $p_{j}$ commute, and their composition $E$ annihilates every blade that anticommutes with some $p_{j}$ and fixes the others, which are, up to sign, the products of the $p_{j}$; their span is the span of the $2^{\ell}$ orthogonal projectors $\Pi_{\chi} = \prod_{j}\tfrac12(1 + \chi_{j}p_{j})$. A fixed element of $\mathcal{K}$ is $c = \sum_{\chi}c_{\chi}\Pi_{\chi}$ with $c_{\chi}\tau(\Pi_{\chi}) = \tau(\Pi_{\chi}c) \ge 0$, because $\tau(\Pi_{\chi}yy^{\dagger}) = \tau((\Pi_{\chi}y)(\Pi_{\chi}y)^{\dagger}) \ge 0$; so an invariant functional is non-negative on $\mathcal{K}$ exactly when it is non-negative on the $\Pi_{\chi}$. For the grading: the grading automorphism $\alpha$ fixes even and negates odd elements and commutes with $\dagger$ (both act on each blade by a sign), so $E = \tfrac12(\mathrm{id} + \alpha)$ is idempotent and commutes with $\dagger$; that $\omega \circ E$ is then the even state agreeing with $\omega$ on even elements is clause (i) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.univalence-even-extension-split}, whose argument uses only this. Moreover, so for $y = y_{0} + y_{1}$ split into even and odd parts $E_{\Gamma}(yy^{\dagger}) = y_{0}y_{0}^{\dagger} + y_{1}y_{1}^{\dagger}$, the cross terms being odd. For a generator $g$, $gg^{\dagger} = gg^{-1} = 1$, so $y_{1}y_{1}^{\dagger} = (y_{1}g)(y_{1}g)^{\dagger}$ with $y_{1}g$ even. So the fixed elements of $\mathcal{K}$ are combinations, with non-negative coefficients, of hermitian squares of even elements, and conversely such combinations are fixed. A functional vanishing on odd elements is invariant, so it is non-negative on $\mathcal{K}$ exactly when it is non-negative on hermitian squares of even elements; normalisation and reality restrict in the obvious way.

\emph{(v).} With $p_{1} = f_{1}e_{1}$: $e_{1}\,e_{2}p_{1} = e_{1}e_{2}f_{1}e_{1} = e_{2}f_{1} = u$ (moving the last $e_{1}$ to the front costs two transpositions), $p_{1}p_{2} = \Gamma$, and the two mixed products $e_{1}p_{2}$ and $p_{1}\,e_{2}p_{1} = e_{2}$ are odd. So $a_{i}b_{j} = x_{i}x'_{j}u + z_{i}z'_{j}\Gamma + (\text{odd})$ and $E_{\Gamma}(a_{i}b_{j}) = x_{i}x'_{j}u + z_{i}z'_{j}\Gamma$; summing with the CHSH signs gives $E_{\Gamma}(C) = Xu + Z\Gamma$. $u^{2} = e_{2}f_{1}e_{2}f_{1} = -e_{2}^{2}f_{1}^{2} = 1$, so $u$ is a blade of square $1$, self-adjoint, and it commutes with $\Gamma$ because it is even. $E_{\Gamma}(a_{i}) = z_{i}p_{1}$ and $E_{\Gamma}(b_{j}) = z'_{j}p_{2}$ ($e_{1}$ and $e_{2}p_{1}$ are odd), whose CHSH element is $Z\Gamma$. For an even state, $\omega(C) = \omega(E_{\Gamma}(C)) = X\omega(u) + Z\omega(\Gamma)$. For self-adjoint $w$ with $w^{2} = 1$, $1 \pm w = \tfrac12(1 \pm w)(1 \pm w)^{\dagger}$ and positivity give $|\omega(w)| \le 1$; hence $|\omega(C)| \le |X| + |Z|$. The four elements $\tfrac14(1 + \epsilon u)(1 + \epsilon'\Gamma)$, $\epsilon, \epsilon' = \pm 1$, are projectors (products of commuting projectors; atoms by clause (i) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.born-weights-under-positivity-a-state-sharp-on-an-atom-is-its-trace-functional}, since the blades commuting with $\Gamma$ are the even ones, and among the bivectors only $e_{2}f_{1} = u$ and $e_{1}f_{2} = \pm u\Gamma$ have square $1$ and commute with $u$: $e_{1}f_{1}$ and $e_{2}f_{2}$ anticommute with $u$, $e_{1}e_{2}$ and $f_{1}f_{2}$ have square $-1$), even, of scalar part $\tfrac14$ because $u$, $\Gamma$ and $u\Gamma$ are non-scalar blades; the state $x \mapsto 4\langle\tfrac14(1 + \epsilon u)(1 + \epsilon'\Gamma)x\rangle_{0}$ is even and has $\omega(u) = \epsilon$, $\omega(\Gamma) = \epsilon'$, so $\omega(C) = \epsilon X + \epsilon'Z$, which is $|X| + |Z|$ for suitable signs. The bound: with the plane vectors $\alpha_{i} = (x_{i}, z_{i})$, $\beta_{j} = (x'_{j}, z'_{j})$ of unit length, $X + Z = \alpha_{1} \cdot (\beta_{1} + \beta_{2}) + \alpha_{2} \cdot (\beta_{1} - \beta_{2})$, so $(X + Z)^{2} \le 2\bigl(|\beta_{1} + \beta_{2}|^{2} + |\beta_{1} - \beta_{2}|^{2}\bigr) = 8$ by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality in $k^{2}$; replacing $z'_{j}$ by $-z'_{j}$ gives the same for $X - Z$, and $|X| + |Z|$ is $|X + Z|$ or $|X - Z|$. The numbers at the stated directions, $X = 1 \cdot (\tfrac35 + \tfrac45) = \tfrac75$ and $Z = 1 \cdot (\tfrac45 + \tfrac35) = \tfrac75$, and the value $\tfrac{14}{5}$, are confirmed by the script.
